title: Catholic: the Hail Mary
hook: a prayer drawn from the angel's and Elizabeth's words to Mary (Luke 1:28, 1:42)

segments.voice: Yesterday: lectio divina, one verse read four times. Your line was read slowly. What did you read twice as slowly? Day two hundred sixty-four.

Two women, one old and one very young, both unexpectedly pregnant. The younger one has just traveled into the hill country to see her older cousin. She walks through the door, says hello, and before she can explain anything, the older woman cries out a blessing, and the baby in her own womb leaps. You probably know the younger one's name: Mary. The older one is Elizabeth. Part of what Elizabeth shouted that day is said by Catholics millions of times, every single day. Today, on our visit to the Catholic tradition: the Hail Mary.
screen: `TWO WOMEN, BOTH EXPECTING.` → `THE BABY LEAPS.` → `SAID MILLIONS OF TIMES A DAY.`

segments.voice: The Hail Mary is built like a mosaic, from pieces of Luke's Gospel. The first piece comes from the angel Gabriel, who visits Mary in Nazareth. In the Douay-Rheims translation, the Catholic English Bible: "Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with thee: blessed art thou among women." The second piece comes from Elizabeth, a few verses later: "Blessed art thou among women, and blessed is the fruit of thy womb." Put them together, add the name Jesus, and you have the first half of the prayer: all of it straight from scripture. The second half is a request, added over the Middle Ages and fixed in its familiar form in the sixteenth century: Mary, the mother of God, is asked to pray for us, now and at the hour of our death. Now look at today's line, full of grace. It comes from a single Greek word Gabriel uses, kecharitomene. You can hear charis inside it, grace, from our week with Christianity. It means something like one who has been graced, favored, filled with favor. The King James Version translates it "highly favoured"; Catholic translations, following Latin, say full of grace. Catholics honor Mary as the mother of Jesus and the first of the saints, and ask her prayers, as they ask the saints'; they're clear that they don't worship her. Orthodox Christians have a similar prayer that begins with the angel's greeting too. Many Protestants honor Mary as a model of faith, reading Luke's words without praying them. For Catholics the Hail Mary is a prayer they learn as children, repeat ten times in each decade of the rosary, and often say at the hour of death.
screen: `THE ANGEL: HAIL, FULL OF GRACE.` · `ELIZABETH: BLESSED ART THOU.` · `THEN A REQUEST: PRAY FOR US.` · `KECHARITOMENE — FILLED WITH FAVOR.` · then, large: `FULL OF GRACE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read it once, slowly. If you pray, you can pray it. If not, just listen to the old greeting as words: hail, full of grace, the Lord is with thee. Then think of someone who has been full of grace toward you, someone who gave more kindness than you earned. Hold them in mind for a few breaths. The bell holds the time.
Catholic, through the Hail Mary: a prayer built from the angel's and Elizabeth's greetings to Mary, then a request for her prayers. Today's word.
Your line: full of grace. Today, greet one person the way Elizabeth greeted Mary: with delight that they walked through the door. Day two hundred sixty-four.

howItsDone: Catholics learn the Hail Mary as children and pray it on its own, in the rosary, and in the Angelus; its first half comes from Luke's Gospel and its second half asks Mary to pray for us.
